techniques.name: Prompt Robustness Testing
techniques.description: Prompt robustness testing measures how much a language model's answers, or its performance on a task, change when the prompt is varied in ways that should not matter, such as rewording, formatting, capitalisation, reordering, or the typos and synonym swaps real users make. The tester starts from task prompts with known correct answers, writes variants that keep the meaning from templates or generates them with perturbation tools such as PromptBench, and runs the model on every variant. Some tools search for the variant that does the most damage, so a drop under that kind of attack is a worst case, not a typical failure rate. The result is reported as the spread of performance across variants, for example the gap between the best and worst format, together with the variants that changed the answer. On one widely used open model, accuracy differed by up to 76 points across formatting changes that kept the meaning, which is why one prompt template is not enough.

example_use_cases.description: A digital health provider testing a symptom-triage chatbot rewrites each benchmark scenario as a brief layperson message, a detailed account, a clinician's summary and an anxious message, and checks that the urgency category stays the same across all four, treating any change as a failure to investigate before release.

A public-sector team choosing between candidate language models for classifying citizen enquiries evaluates each across a set of plausible prompt formats and instruction paraphrases, and compares models on worst-format and average accuracy rather than on a single prompt, because the ranking of models can change with the template.

A bank validating a model that summarises suspicious-transaction reports checks that the risk category it extracts does not change when the same activity is described with different terminology, abbreviations or layout, as reports from different branches would be.

limitations.description: The space of possible prompt variants is unbounded, so a test samples it. A model can pass on every variant tried and still fail on a phrasing nobody generated, and the conclusion holds only for the kinds of variation the test set covers.

Whether a variant keeps the meaning of the original is a judgement. Automated perturbations can change meaning or produce text no user would write, and attack-based tools search for the most damaging variant, so their drops are worst cases. Variant sets need checking by someone who knows the domain.

Results do not transfer between models: which formats work well correlated only weakly across models in a large study, and robustness to one domain's phrasing says little about another's. The test has to be rerun for each model version, each prompt template change and each domain.

Every variant multiplies the number of model calls, and for open-ended answers each response may need scoring by a domain expert rather than against a fixed label. Testing many formats across many examples and candidate models quickly becomes costly.

It shows that outputs are brittle, not why. Choosing the best-scoring template on the same variants used to test it gives an optimistic estimate of how that template will perform on new inputs, so template selection and the final robustness measurement need separate data.

resources.title: PromptRobust: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Large Language Models on Adversarial Prompts
resources.abstract: The increasing reliance on Large Language Models (LLMs) across academia and industry necessitates a comprehensive understanding of their robustness to prompts. In response to this vital need, we introduce PromptRobust, a robustness benchmark designed to measure LLMs' resilience to adversarial prompts. This study uses a plethora of adversarial textual attacks targeting prompts across multiple levels: character, word, sentence, and semantic. The adversarial prompts, crafted to mimic plausible user errors like typos or synonyms, aim to evaluate how slight deviations can affect LLM outcomes while maintaining semantic integrity. These prompts are then employed in diverse tasks including sentiment analysis, natural language inference, reading comprehension, machine translation, and math problem-solving. Our study generates 4, 788 adversarial prompts, meticulously evaluated over 8 tasks and 13 datasets. Our findings demonstrate that contemporary LLMs are not robust to adversarial prompts. Furthermore, we present comprehensive analysis to understand the mystery behind prompt robustness and its transferability. We then offer insightful robustness analysis, beneficial to both researchers and everyday users. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/promptbench.

resources.title: State of What Art? A Call for Multi-Prompt LLM Evaluation
resources.abstract: Recent advances in LLMs have led to an abundance of evaluation benchmarks, which typically rely on a single instruction template per task. We create a large-scale collection of instruction paraphrases and comprehensively analyze the brittleness introduced by single-prompt evaluations across 6.5M instances, involving 20 different LLMs and 39 tasks from 3 benchmarks. We find that different instruction templates lead to very different performance, both absolute and relative. Instead, we propose a set of diverse metrics on multiple instruction paraphrases, specifically tailored for different use cases (e.g., LLM vs. downstream development), ensuring a more reliable and meaningful assessment of LLM capabilities. We show that our metrics provide new insights into the strengths and limitations of current LLMs.

Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
resources.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

resources.title: Prompt sensitivity of large language models in orthodontic patient counseling: a scenario-based experimental study
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as accessible sources of health information, including orthodontic patient counseling. While previous studies have evaluated the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated responses, the effect of prompt formulation on the safety and quality of orthodontic advice remains unclear. Understanding prompt sensitivity is essential for assessing the real-world reliability of conversational AI systems, as patient queries are typically expressed in diverse linguistic forms. METHODS: This in silico experimental study evaluated prompt sensitivity using 24 standardized orthodontic clinical scenarios. Each scenario was queried using four prompt formulations (brief layperson, detailed patient, professional clinical, and anxiety-driven), resulting in 96 prompts. These were submitted to four LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude), generating 384 responses. Responses were independently evaluated by two orthodontic experts using a predefined expert scoring rubric across accuracy, safety, completeness, and clarity. Consensus scores were analyzed using the Friedman test for prompt effects and the Kruskal-Wallis test for model comparisons. Unsafe response rates and prompt robustness indices were also calculated. RESULTS: Safety scores did not differ significantly across prompt formulations (χ²(3) = 3.40, p = 0.334) or between models (H = 0.17, p = 0.982). A total of 5 of 384 responses (1.3%) were classified as unsafe. Prompt robustness analysis demonstrated low variability (mean prompt robustness index = 0.15). Response length differed significantly across prompt types (p = 0.0029), whereas response time did not (p = 0.998). A significant difference in clarity scores was observed across models (p = 0.029), with post hoc analysis indicating higher clarity scores for ChatGPT than Claude (adjusted p = 0.020). CONCLUSIONS: LLMs demonstrated consistent and clinically safe performance in orthodontic patient counseling, with minimal sensitivity to prompt formulation. While prompt wording influenced response length, it did not affect clinical reliability. Differences between models were primarily related to clarity rather than content. LLMs may provide stable informational support across diverse patient queries; however, their outputs should remain adjunctive to professional care.

techniques.name: Continual Learning Stability Testing
techniques.description: Continual learning stability testing checks whether a model that is updated over time with new data or tasks keeps what it learned earlier, by scoring it after each update on a test set for every task in the sequence. Backward transfer is the average change in accuracy on earlier tasks, and a large fall is called catastrophic forgetting. Forward transfer is accuracy on a task the model has not yet been trained on, compared with an untrained model. Scoring only at the end of each update can hide a sharp but temporary drop, so stricter tests also score the model during training and report its worst result. The scores can also show whether methods meant to protect old knowledge, such as replaying stored examples of earlier data or penalising changes to the weights that matter for earlier tasks, are working.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team retrains its abuse classifier every month on newly reported content. Before release it scores the new version on a held-out test set for each earlier abuse type and holds the release if detection of any type has fallen by more than the agreed margin.

A hospital team lets a triage model keep learning from new cases while it is in use. Because users meet any dip as it happens, the team scores the model on its urgent conditions at regular points during each update, not only at the end, and stops the update if the lowest score falls below the agreed floor.

A bank updates its fraud model weekly on newly confirmed cases. To see whether replaying stored examples of older fraud actually protects detection of old patterns, the team runs the same update with and without replay and compares how well each version still catches each earlier fraud type.

A factory retrains a camera-based hazard detector when a new machine is installed. Before it returns to the line, the safety engineer scores the retrained detector on the stored test images for every previously known hazard and signs off only if none is detected less reliably than before.

limitations.description: Every update means scoring the model on a test set for each earlier task, so total cost grows with the number of tasks as well as the number of updates. Old test sets also have to be kept, which can conflict with data-retention rules, and scoring only a sample of tasks cannot detect forgetting in the rest.

Scores taken only at the end of each update can miss a sharp, temporary drop on earlier tasks while the model is still learning. This matters for a system that stays in service during training, because users meet the dip. Catching it needs repeated scoring during training, which adds to the cost.

Stability scores measure only one side of the stability-plasticity trade-off. A model can score perfectly on earlier tasks by refusing to learn anything new, so results must be read alongside accuracy on the new tasks.

Deciding how much forgetting is acceptable depends on the application, and the test cannot settle it. A threshold set too tight blocks adaptation to changing conditions, and one set too loose lets real losses through.

Results hold for the sequence of tasks tested, and assume tasks with clear boundaries and a labelled test set for each. Real data streams often drift gradually, and how much a model forgets depends on how different consecutive tasks are, so a gentler test sequence understates forgetting.

resources.title: Continual evaluation for lifelong learning: Identifying the stability gap
resources.abstract: Time-dependent data-generating distributions have proven to be difficult for gradient-based training of neural networks, as the greedy updates result in catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge. Despite the progress in the field of continual learning to overcome this forgetting, we show that a set of common state-of-the-art methods still suffers from substantial forgetting upon starting to learn new tasks, except that this forgetting is temporary and followed by a phase of performance recovery. We refer to this intriguing but potentially problematic phenomenon as the stability gap. The stability gap had likely remained under the radar due to standard practice in the field of evaluating continual learning models only after each task. Instead, we establish a framework for continual evaluation that uses per-iteration evaluation and we define a new set of metrics to quantify worst-case performance. Empirically we show that experience replay, constraint-based replay, knowledge-distillation, and parameter regularization methods are all prone to the stability gap; and that the stability gap can be observed in class-, task-, and domain-incremental learning benchmarks. Additionally, a controlled experiment shows that the stability gap increases when tasks are more dissimilar. Finally, by disentangling gradients into plasticity and stability components, we propose a conceptual explanation for the stability gap.

resources.title: Gradient Episodic Memory for Continual Learning
resources.abstract: One major obstacle towards AI is the poor ability of models to solve new problems quicker, and without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. To better understand this issue, we study the problem of continual learning, where the model observes, once and one by one, examples concerning a sequence of tasks. First, we propose a set of metrics to evaluate models learning over a continuum of data. These metrics characterize models not only by their test accuracy, but also in terms of their ability to transfer knowledge across tasks. Second, we propose a model for continual learning, called Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) that alleviates forgetting, while allowing beneficial transfer of knowledge to previous tasks. Our experiments on variants of the MNIST and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate the strong performance of GEM when compared to the state-of-the-art.

resources.title: Development and validation of deep continual learning model to sequentially learn multiple clinical prediction tasks for ICU patients
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND ICU patients often suffer from critical and complex condition, and multiple potential risks should be monitored to provide them comprehensive care. However, no study proposes continual learning (CL) model that can effectively solve multiple clinical prediction tasks without catastrophic forgetting. This study proposes three deep CL models for ICU patients. METHODS Three public ICU databases were employed. The included patients from MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV were divided into eight task sets, and the patients from eICU-CRD composed the test set. We propose three CL models (CL_1, CL_2, CL_3) to sequentially learn eight prediction tasks on the eight task sets, and then externally validate them on the test set. We compare our models to three representative baseline CL models and the single-task (ST) and multi-task (MT) model. We train all the CL models under different orders, and evaluate their prediction performance by multiple metrics and their memory ability by backward transfer (BWT). We also analyzed the effect of previously learned tasks on learning new tasks. RESULTS Our three CL models had comparable or slightly weaker performance compared to ST and MT model on the eight tasks. They effectively mitigated catastrophic forgetting, and their performance is robust to different training orders. CL_2 and CL_3 even have improved performance on the current task after learning some previous tasks. Our three CL models outperformed the baseline CL models in most experiments. CONCLUSIONS Our CL models are promising to sequentially learn multiple clinical prediction tasks for ICU patients. The CL_2 and CL_3 show the ability of utilizing information of previous tasks to improve learning new tasks. More new datasets and tasks are still needed to further verify the validity of the CL models.

techniques.name: Few-Shot Fairness Evaluation
techniques.description: Few-shot fairness evaluation assesses whether in-context learning with few-shot examples introduces or amplifies biases in model predictions. This technique systematically varies demographic characteristics in few-shot examples and measures how these variations affect model outputs for different groups. Evaluation includes testing prompt sensitivity (how example selection impacts fairness), stereotype amplification (whether biased examples disproportionately affect outputs), and consistency (whether similar inputs receive equitable treatment regardless of example composition).

example_use_cases.description: Testing whether a resume screening LLM's few-shot examples inadvertently introduce gender bias by showing more male examples for technical positions, affecting how it evaluates subsequent applicants.
Ensuring a customer service classifier maintains reliable performance across demographic groups regardless of which few-shot examples users or developers choose to include in prompts.
Documenting how few-shot example selection affects fairness metrics, transparently reporting sensitivity to example composition in deployment guidelines.

Evaluating whether a medical triage LLM's few-shot examples for symptom assessment inadvertently encode demographic biases (e.g., more examples of cardiac symptoms in male patients), leading to differential urgency assessments across patient populations.

Testing whether few-shot examples used in a legal case summarization system introduce racial or socioeconomic bias in how defendant backgrounds or case circumstances are characterized, affecting case outcome predictions.

Assessing whether few-shot examples in a loan application review assistant systematically present more favourable examples for certain demographic profiles, biasing the model's assessment of creditworthiness for subsequent applications.

Verifying that an automated essay grading system maintains consistent standards across student demographics when few-shot examples inadvertently represent particular writing styles, dialects, or cultural references more prominently.

limitations.description: Vast number of possible few-shot example combinations makes exhaustive testing infeasible, requiring sampling strategies that may miss important configurations.
Fairness may be highly sensitive to subtle differences in example wording or formatting, making it difficult to provide robust guarantees.
Trade-offs between example diversity and task performance may force choices between fairness and accuracy.
Results may not generalise across different prompt templates or instruction formats, requiring separate evaluation for each prompting strategy.
Requires carefully labeled datasets with demographic annotations to measure fairness across groups, which may be unavailable, expensive to create, or raise privacy concerns in sensitive domains.
Designing representative test sets that capture realistic few-shot example distributions requires deep domain expertise and understanding of how the system will be used in practice.
Evaluating fairness across multiple demographic groups with various few-shot configurations can be computationally expensive, particularly for large language models with high inference costs.

resources.title: Fairness-guided few-shot prompting for large language models
resources.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated surprising ability to perform in-context learning, i.e., these models can be directly applied to solve numerous downstream tasks by conditioning on a prompt constructed by a few input-output examples. However, prior research has shown that in-context learning can suffer from high instability due to variations in training examples, example order, and prompt formats. Therefore, the construction of an appropriate prompt is essential for improving the performance of in-context learning. In this paper, we revisit this problem from the view of predictive bias. Specifically, we introduce a metric to evaluate the predictive bias of a fixed prompt against labels or a given attributes. Then we empirically show that prompts with higher bias always lead to unsatisfactory predictive quality. Based on this observation, we propose a novel search strategy based on the greedy search to identify the near-optimal prompt for improving the performance of in-context learning. We perform comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art mainstream models such as GPT-3 on various downstream tasks. Our results indicate that our method can enhance the model's in-context learning performance in an effective and interpretable manner.

resources.abstract: Recent studies highlight the effectiveness of using in-context learning (ICL) to steer large language models (LLMs) in processing tabular data, a challenging task given the structured nature of such data.Despite advancements in performance, the fairness implications of these methods are less understood.This study investigates how varying demonstrations within ICL prompts influence the fairness outcomes of LLMs.Our findings reveal that deliberately including minority group samples in prompts significantly boosts fairness without sacrificing predictive accuracy.Further experiments demonstrate that the proportion of minority to majority samples in demonstrations affects the trade-off between fairness and prediction accuracy.Based on these insights, we introduce a mitigation technique that employs clustering and evolutionary strategies to curate a diverse and representative sample set from the training data.This approach aims to enhance both predictive performance and fairness in ICL applications.Experimental results validate that our proposed method dramatically improves fairness across various metrics, showing its efficacy in real-world scenarios.

techniques.name: Multi-Agent System Testing
techniques.description: Multi-agent system testing examines systems in which several AI agents act on shared tasks or resources, to find failures that no single agent shows on its own. Testers run the agents together in simulated or scripted scenarios, often with injected faults such as failed sensors, delayed messages or conflicting goals, and record the failures that appear. Checks cover whether the task is completed, whether coordination breaks down (for example through deadlock, collisions or one agent's error spreading to others), and whether stated safety rules are ever broken. For language-model agents, benchmarks such as MultiAgentBench score task completion and the quality of collaboration or competition. For small or abstract models, a model checker such as MCMAS can search every reachable state for a violation of a rule written in formal logic and, for many kinds of rule, return an example run that breaks it.

example_use_cases.description: A logistics firm models its warehouse robots' movement rules in a model checker and asks whether two robots can ever occupy the same aisle cell or wait on each other forever. Any counterexample the checker returns is a concrete sequence of events that engineers replay in simulation before the control software goes live.

A city traffic authority testing coordinated intersection controllers injects sensor failures and conflicting local objectives in a simulator. It checks whether emergency vehicles still get priority and traffic flow stays within agreed limits, and decides from the results whether the system can go to a pilot corridor.

A trading firm's risk team runs all of its cooperating trading agents together in a market simulator replaying a high-volatility day. It checks whether their combined orders breach position limits or form patterns that compliance would treat as manipulation, and whether one agent's failure spreads to the others.

A software company building a team of language-model agents to fix bugs (a planner, a coder and a reviewer) runs the team on a benchmark of shared coding tasks under different coordination layouts, such as a chain or a star. It compares task completion and coordination scores before choosing a layout for production.

limitations.description: The number of possible interactions grows explosively with the number of agents, so tests sample a tiny part of the space. A clean run shows that the scenarios tried did not fail, not that none will, and the gap widens as agents are added.

Model checking needs a formal model of each agent and its environment, and the answer is only as good as that model. Large state spaces limit how many agents it can handle, and agents that learn and change behaviour are hard to capture, so it is usually combined with simulation testing.

Benchmark scores for communication and planning come from a language model acting as judge on a coarse five-point scale, so they inherit its biases. A high coordination score does not show that a safety property holds.

Simulators simplify real conditions such as communication delays, sensor noise and physical or social dynamics, and realistic simulation is costly to build and needs domain modelling expertise. Failures that occur only in the real environment will not appear.

Tests and model checks find only the failures the testers specify. A hazard that no one wrote a safety rule or scenario for is not tested, and rules written in temporal logic need specialist skill to state correctly.

resources.title: MCMAS: an open-source model checker for the verification of multi-agent systems
resources.abstract: We present MCMAS, a model checker for the verification of multi-agent systems. MCMAS supports efficient symbolic techniques for the verification of multi-agent systems against specifications representing temporal, epistemic and strategic properties. We present the underlying semantics of the specification language supported and the algorithms implemented in MCMAS, including its fairness and counterexample generation features. We provide a detailed description of the implementation. We illustrate its use by discussing a number of examples and evaluate its performance by comparing it against other model checkers for multi-agent systems on a common case study.

resources.title: MultiAgentBench : Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities as autonomous agents, yet existing benchmarks either focus on single-agent tasks or are confined to narrow domains, failing to capture the dynamics of multi-agent coordination and competition. In this paper, we introduce MultiAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems across diverse, interactive scenarios. Our framework measures not only task completion but also the quality of collaboration and competition using novel, milestone-based key performance indicators. Moreover, we evaluate various coordination protocols (including star, chain, tree, and graph topologies) and innovative strategies such as group discussion and cognitive planning. Notably, gpt-4o-mini reaches the average highest task score, graph structure performs the best among coordination protocols in the research scenario, and cognitive planning improves milestone achievement rates by 3%. Code and datasets are public available at https://github.com/MultiagentBench/MARBLE.

resources.title: RV4JaCa - Towards Runtime Verification of Multi-Agent Systems and Robotic Applications
resources.abstract: This paper presents a Runtime Verification (RV) approach for Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) using the JaCaMo framework. Our objective is to bring a layer of security to the MAS. This is achieved keeping in mind possible safety-critical uses of the MAS, such as robotic applications. This layer is capable of controlling events during the execution of the system without needing a specific implementation in the behaviour of each agent to recognise the events. In this paper, we mainly focus on MAS when used in the context of hybrid intelligence. This use requires communication between software agents and human beings. In some cases, communication takes place via natural language dialogues. However, this kind of communication brings us to a concern related to controlling the flow of dialogue so that agents can prevent any change in the topic of discussion that could impair their reasoning. The latter may be a problem and undermine the development of the software agents. In this paper, we tackle this problem by proposing and demonstrating the implementation of a framework that aims to control the dialogue flow in a MAS; especially when the MAS communicates with the user through natural language to aid decision-making in a hospital bed allocation scenario.

techniques.name: Linear Bound Propagation Verification
techniques.description: Linear bound propagation verification proves that a trained neural network meets a stated property for every input in a defined region, for example that no small change to the pixels of an image alters its class, or that a controller's output stays within limits across a box of sensor readings. CROWN, the named method, replaces each neuron's activation function with two straight lines that bound it from above and below over the values that neuron can take, then works backwards from the outputs through the layers to express an upper and a lower bound on each output as a linear function of the input, and evaluates those functions over the region to obtain guaranteed numerical bounds. If the bounds show the property holds (for a classifier, that the correct class's score stays above every other class's), it is proved for the whole region; because the straight lines over-approximate the network, bounds that fail to show it leave the case undecided, so bound propagation on its own is sound but incomplete. The alpha-beta-CROWN tool tightens the bounds by tuning the lines with gradient-based optimisation and by branch and bound: for a ReLU network it splits undecided neurons into their active and inactive cases and bounds each part separately, which given enough time settles every case, making the tool complete for ReLU networks, but at a cost that can grow exponentially with the number of neurons split, so in practice each run ends as verified, falsified (a counterexample input found) or timed out. Running on graphics processors, it reaches convolutional networks with millions of parameters, larger than exact constraint solvers usually handle, at the price of leaving hard cases undecided.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics supplier's verification team checks the network that flags wildfires in airborne infrared images. For each background crop in a held-out set taken from real flight logs, it uses alpha-beta-CROWN to prove that the detector's confidence never falls as a planted fire signal grows stronger within the specified range, lists the crops where a counterexample is found, and enters the proved cases in the safety case as evidence for that consistency requirement.

A transmission system operator replaces slow time-domain simulation with a neural network that predicts whether the grid stays stable after a fault, inside the optimiser that plans generator dispatch. At each candidate dispatch its engineers use alpha-beta-CROWN to certify that the stability prediction holds for every combination of wind, solar and load within the forecast uncertainty, and raise the stability margin wherever certification fails before the plan is issued.

A pharmaceutical packaging line uses a convolutional classifier to accept or reject blister packs from camera images. Before each model release the quality team reports certified accuracy on held-out images: the share for which CROWN bounds prove that no change of up to 2/255 in any pixel can flip the decision, a bound set above the largest per-pixel noise measured on the line's cameras. A release whose certified accuracy falls well below its ordinary accuracy goes back for retraining.

limitations.description: Bound propagation on its own is incomplete: when the bounds are too loose to show the property, the case stays undecided, which is not evidence either way. Branch and bound settles more cases, but the problem is NP-complete in general, so hard cases end in a time-out. In an industrial study of an airborne wildfire detector, every query for a monotonicity property was settled, while 62 per cent of the queries for a sensor-blur property timed out.

The property must be written as a region of inputs, such as every image within a small per-pixel change of a test image or a box of sensor values, plus a linear condition on the outputs. Rotation, lighting, weather or blur are not regions of that kind; covering them means modelling them first, for example with a separate network that generates plausible blur, and the accuracy of that model then has to be argued separately.

Robustness is proved one region at a time, usually around each test input, so certified accuracy on a test set is evidence about those inputs and that perturbation only. It does not carry over to new inputs from operation, and a classifier certified around every test image can still misclassify an unperturbed image it has not seen.

It needs the whole network in a supported form (PyTorch or ONNX) and, beyond small networks, a graphics processor with enough memory: most of the tool's example configurations were tested on a 24 GB GPU, and its documented branch-and-bound support for ReLU image models reaches residual networks of about 20 layers. Layers the library does not support need their bounds written by hand, and its documented reach of millions of parameters is far below the size of large language models.

The guarantee covers the network alone. Pre-processing, sensor faults and, for a controller, the plant it drives and how errors build up over time are outside it, so a proof that a policy network never outputs an unsafe command for any state in a box does not show that the controlled system stays safe; that needs a separate analysis of the closed loop.

resources.title: Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification with General Activation Functions
resources.abstract: Finding minimum distortion of adversarial examples and thus certifying robustness in neural networks classifiers is known to be a challenging problem. Nevertheless, recently it has been shown to be possible to give a non-trivial certified lower bound of minimum distortion, and some recent progress has been made towards this direction by exploiting the piece-wise linear nature of ReLU activations. However, a generic robustness certification for \textit{general} activation functions still remains largely unexplored. To address this issue, in this paper we introduce CROWN, a general framework to certify robustness of neural networks with general activation functions. The novelty in our algorithm consists of bounding a given activation function with linear and quadratic functions, hence allowing it to tackle general activation functions including but not limited to the four popular choices: ReLU, tanh, sigmoid and arctan. In addition, we facilitate the search for a tighter certified lower bound by \textit{adaptively} selecting appropriate surrogates for each neuron activation. Experimental results show that CROWN on ReLU networks can notably improve the certified lower bounds compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithm Fast-Lin, while having comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, CROWN also demonstrates its effectiveness and flexibility on networks with general activation functions, including tanh, sigmoid and arctan.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Metamorphic Testing
techniques.description: Metamorphic testing checks a model or AI system without needing the correct output for each test input, by checking that the outputs for related inputs stand in a relation that must hold if the system works as intended. The tester first writes metamorphic relations from knowledge of the task, each pairing a change to the input with the change it should cause in the output, or with no change: adding fog to a road image should leave a steering prediction within a set tolerance, adding a few stray sensor points outside the road area should not remove any detected obstacle, and rotating a whole flight scenario should leave its outcome unchanged. Existing test inputs (source cases) are transformed into follow-up inputs according to each relation, the system is run on both, and each pair is checked, with numeric outputs often allowed a tolerance. A violation points to a fault or unwanted behaviour without any labelled answer, unless the relation itself is wrong; the output is the violation rate for each relation with the failing pairs, and a relation that holds on every pair shows only that the outputs agree with each other, not that they are right. Prompt robustness testing and causal discrimination testing in this catalogue each apply one family of invariance relations (meaning-preserving changes to a prompt, and a change of protected attribute), and prompt robustness testing also scores the answers against known ones; metamorphic testing is the general procedure for writing and checking any such relation, including relations that say how the output should change, and needs no known answers.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider evaluating a machine-learning conflict-detection aid for en-route controllers has no ground truth for most replayed traffic samples. Its test team writes three relations: swapping two aircraft's call signs, shifting every timestamp by the same amount, and rotating the whole sample together with its wind field must not change which aircraft pairs are flagged. It runs them on a year of recorded traffic and holds the release until every violation is explained.

A supplier of lidar obstacle perception for driverless shuttles cannot label every frame it records. Following a relation implied by the perception specification, its test team adds a few hundred random points outside the mapped road area to recorded frames and checks that no obstacle detected in the original frame disappears, reporting the share of frames where one does, by number of points added, as a release criterion for each software build.

A weather service testing a neural network that nowcasts rainfall from radar images checks a relation expected from the way rain moves with the wind: away from the domain's edges, shifting the input radar sequence a few grid cells east should shift the forecast rain field by the same amount, within a tolerance set from the model's day-to-day error. Forecasters review the breaking cases to judge whether the model has learnt a dependence on location, such as on terrain, that it should keep.

A bank moving its credit-scoring models to a new library cannot treat every difference from the old library's outputs as a fault, since the solvers differ. Its validation team writes relations the mathematics guarantees: reordering the input columns, or adding a constant to a numeric input in training and scoring data of a logistic regression with an unpenalised intercept, must leave every predicted probability unchanged within solver tolerance. Each violation is investigated as a fault.

limitations.description: Passing shows that outputs are consistent, not that they are correct. A model that gives the same wrong answer for a source case and its follow-up satisfies the relation, and one that is wrong in the same way everywhere can pass every invariance relation. On its own the technique therefore does not suit systems where each output must be shown to be right, and it complements rather than replaces testing against known answers where those exist.

The evidence is only as good as the relations, which are written by hand from domain knowledge, with no systematic way to choose among the many possible ones. A relation the system is not bound to obey produces false alarms: in a study of the Weka library, violations by its nearest-neighbour classifier came from legitimate tie-breaking between equally likely labels, not from faults. An incomplete set of relations gives false confidence.

Most model outputs need a tolerance, and the result depends heavily on it. In the DeepTest study of three driving models, violations under simple image transformations fell from 23,391 when a transformed frame's squared error against the human steering label could be at most the original mean squared error to 330 when it could be five times that, and manual review still found false positives. Counts compare only between runs with the same tolerance, set from what the application can accept.

Follow-up inputs are synthetic and may not occur in practice: rain or fog added to an image, or points scattered into a lidar frame, approximate real conditions without reproducing them. A violation on an unrealistic input may not matter in operation, and a pass covers only the transformations tried, so the evidence is about the tested relations and transformations, not the operating conditions as a whole.

A model whose outputs vary between runs on the same input, through sampling, seeds or GPU arithmetic, breaks relations by chance, so runs must be made repeatable or each case repeated and judged statistically. This bites hardest for relations over the training data, such as Xie et al.'s for classifiers, which need the model retrained for every follow-up case; for models that are costly to train only prediction-time relations are practical, and they test the trained model, not its training.

resources.title: Metamorphic Testing: A New Approach for Generating Next Test Cases
resources.abstract: In software testing, a set of test cases is constructed according to some predefined selection criteria. The software is then examined against these test cases. Three interesting observations have been made on the current artifacts of software testing. Firstly, an error-revealing test case is considered useful while a successful test case which does not reveal software errors is usually not further investigated. Whether these successful test cases still contain useful information for revealing software errors has not been properly studied. Secondly, no matter how extensive the testing has been conducted in the development phase, errors may still exist in the software [5]. These errors, if left undetected, may eventually cause damage to the production system. The study of techniques for uncovering software errors in the production phase is seldom addressed in the literature. Thirdly, as indicated by Weyuker in [6], the availability of test oracles is pragmatically unattainable in most situations. However, the availability of test oracles is generally assumed in conventional software testing techniques. In this paper, we propose a novel test case selection technique that derives new test cases from the successful ones. The selection aims at revealing software errors that are possibly left undetected in successful test cases which may be generated using some existing strategies. As such, the proposed technique augments the effectiveness of existing test selection strategies. The technique also helps uncover software errors in the production phase and can be used in the absence of test oracles.
